title: Has anyone actually built a profitable AI trading bot using ChatGPT, Codex, TradingView, Binance, or Bybit?
author: Overall_Relief_8716
selftext:
Every day on TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube, I see people claiming they've turned $50–$300 into thousands within weeks using AI trading bots or automated strategies.

But there's always a catch. You're told to comment a keyword, wait for a DM, buy a course, or pay for access to some secret trading prompt.

I'm genuinely curious: **Has anyone here actually built an AI trading bot that consistently makes money using real market conditions?**

I have access to ChatGPT Pro and Codex, and I'm interested in building something that can trade automatically on Binance or Bybit, potentially using TradingView signals, Python, APIs, or AI-generated strategies.

I'm not looking for someone selling a course or promising guaranteed profits. I'm trying to understand whether there's a legitimate, tested approach that actually works.

A few questions:

1. Has anyone successfully built an automated trading bot using ChatGPT or Codex?
2. Are there any strategies, prompts, or open-source GitHub projects worth exploring?
3. Can AI realistically analyze market conditions, open and close trades, manage stop-losses, and improve its strategy over time?
4. Has anyone tested such a bot with real money for several months and achieved consistent profitability after fees?
5. If you were starting with $100–$300, how would you approach building and testing a fully automated trading system?

**I'm especially interested in hearing from people who have actually built and tested something, not influencers promoting unrealistic returns.**

If you've built something that works, I'd appreciate hearing about your approach, tools, results, and lessons learned. Even if it failed, I'd be interested in understanding why.

Let's have a genuine discussion about what's actually possible with AI trading in 2026.

I'm still looking into it, but that's all that i've found so far.

comments.author: fleatedplutmting
comments.body:
I think the biggest misconception here is that AI somehow gives you a trading edge. It doesn't. What it does give you is the ability to build, test and refine strategies that would've required a pretty decent programming background a few years ago.

The hard part isn't building the bot anymore, it's finding a strategy that actually works consistently. Anyone can backtest something against historical data and make the results look incredible. Getting those same results in live markets is a completely different story

Many projects are giving everyday traders the ability to build, backtest and eventually lease out their own AI trading bots without needing to be programmers themselves.

Personally, I think this is where things are heading. Not AI magically predicting every market move, but giving ordinary traders access to tools that were previously reserved for people with serious technical knowledge and resources

And whatever you do, stay well away from anyone promising guaranteed returns. That's usually where the BS starts.

comments.author: fomoz
comments.body:
I built a platform where users can run their own AI trading bots for free. Pretty much any provider, local AI, and you can also use your Codex, Claude Code, Gemini, Grok or other subscriptions to run inference as well (since monthly AI plans are heavily subsidized).

The issue I have with my own bots is that they do well in a trending market (30 to 100% ROI per month, depending on leverage), but they still bleed in chop. I'm setting up some backtesting capabilities over MCP where you can test out different bot settings (prompts, etc.) in difficult historical scenarios and tweak.

You can do this fully autonomously, for example Claude Code Opus 5.5 is guiding the experiments on my fleet over MCP, collects samples and tries permutations of different settings (temperature, cadence, prompt tweaks).

This takes time, but I think it's much more efficient than running a long back test that's gonna take a weeks to a month to test a month of market action. I'm looking for difficult scenarios where bots lose money vs times where they take no action (as they should).

Also, I support many crypto exchanges, both CEX and DEX. Binance included.

For classic algo trading, I agree that the edge usually fades. It's not hand off for years, you're usually tweaking it pretty often.

For AI trading, I don't know. I think it's possible to create a general strategy that just works. Same as a legendary trader (think PTJ, Soros), they were able to adapt.

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body: For the “improve its strategy over time” part, I would version the model, prompt and rules together and keep a frozen baseline. A useful first milestone is reproducible decisions and bounded exposure in paper trading, before evaluating any profitability claim.

comments.author: antoniusbethyname
comments.body:
I built one that isn’t agentic as in it doesn’t require AI to operate but AI built the code. Super simple system actually. Built and back tested using 8 or 9 years of 1m bars on ES.

Forward deployment on paper trading test including estimated slippage from futures shows about 20% return on the starting balance over the last 3 months with approx 5% blended drawdown. Couple of those weeks were atrociously low volume chop. Really the last couple months have been not a great trading environment for the system and it’s still doing good. So far it’s not as great as the backtest but still awesome and too early to tell.

. Looking to deploy it for real on 10k running 2 MES contracts then if it looks as good as the forward test I’ll probably throw 100k at it and run 2 ES.

**Factors to keep in mind:** running 1256 contracts like futures and European style cash settled index options is 60/40 long term/short term cap gains tax. Meaning it will be around a blended 30% tax. You have to factor in tax drag.

What this means is if you make 10k off of 100k (10% returns) just chilling in the index and not trading, you’d need just over 14k of 1256 contract gains to match that 10k just sitting in the index left alone to compound after taxes are factored in. Yes If you sold and paid long term cap gains on the 10k it would be around 8k net (20% LTCG tax) but you can just leave it and let it compound around 10% per year. 1256 contact gains will be taxed every year regardless because they’re mark to market taxation.

Different story if you have better drawdown/sharpe/calmer ratios or better performance in times of market underperformance. Raw comparison of gains isn’t always the best measurement but you get the point.

# Short version: Make sure your system not only beats the market but beats it by enough to justify the taxes.

# Also no I’m not sharing the system don’t ask.

comments.author: DB4SS
comments.body:
Yes, but it's only been running live for 2 months which is not enough time to come to serious conclusions. Also it only works because I already had ideas I wanted to test, after years of discretionary trading. 

Asking AI to trade for you will result in it asking questions that you'll need to answer, like why, when, how big... These are things that need to be backtested. I don't think the power of AI is in getting it to trade for you, it's benefit is the rapid iteration of prototypes. You can use it to learn more about your strategy and understand why it is, or isn't working.

I would also say that AI is probably really well suited for digesting news articles that come out, but I really doubt there's much alpha in that for short term trading. It's probably priced in already by the time the article is published lol. 

All that said if you extend your trade duration, into more of a swing trading style, using very conservative leverage (quarter Kelly), then you can make any strategy with a positive expectancy work.

Just be curious, use the AI to assist in the creation of your vision. Don't just ask it for the god-tier trading system, because it won't have one (yet). Also that trading account is way too small, you need to scrape together much more money, otherwise it's a lot of time spent on developing a trading strategy, but it will take years before it's bringing in meaningfully returns.

If you are asking if I have used Claude to analyze existing (built two years ago) bots executed on Option Alpha and refine them, then Hell Yes! Let me answer your questions.

1. Has anyone successfully built an automated trading bot using ChatGPT or Codex?

Yes. Claude manages changes to my Option Alpha bots. It has also built additional bots for paper trading.

2. Are there any strategies, prompts, or open-source GitHub projects worth exploring?

I have no clue.

3. Can AI realistically analyze market conditions, open and close trades, manage stop-losses, and improve its strategy over time?

Not for me, but it can analyze parameters of an existing strategy and test it in different regimes.

4. Has anyone tested such a bot with real money for several months and achieved consistent profitability after fees?

Absolutely. My typical CAGR is about 30%. I was previously sustaining 40% or so, but Claude backtesting (Via QuantConnect) discovered that 2020 COVID volatility spikes would have wiped me out. The strategy adjustments that would survive COVID now makes about 30% CAGR. Today my three live bots generated $4,975 in profit, which is higher than a typical day.

5. If you were starting with $100–$300, how would you approach building and testing a fully automated trading system?

I cannot help here. My strategies assume a starting capital of $50,000 per bot.

comments.author: Few-Instruction-2087
comments.body: I've used Claude to code a few strategies for ninjatrader to trade futures which so have a positive expectancy and I'm in the process of forward testing now. I will say, it can't just magically give you profitable strategies if you don't know what direction to point it in. You also need a lot of data from a platform like databento. Some of the edges you find in formats like orderflow will be real but retail traders simply don't have the technology/access/speed to exploit it. Commissions/spreads destroy most strategies. 99.9% of retail strats don't work with automated configs; that's not to say they aren't profitable but they require discretion to work. You need strict tests to prove any strat is not luck (look into stuff like welch, coin flip etc). Use concept drift detection to detect fading edges and working strats will require some implementation of mathematical/statistical concepts. I would love to just say what edges I've found but generally people don't give away their edges because it basically speeds up how fast it can fade.

comments.author: Individual_Dare_5583
comments.body:
I’ve experienced something interesting building my own trading systems.  
I have a discretionary strategy that’s produced a 70–80% win rate in my trading, but when I translate the same underlying concepts into a fully mechanical system, performance drops to roughly 50/50 and breakeven.  
That’s taught me something important.. the setup itself isn’t necessarily the entire edge.  
A significant part of the edge may come from knowing when NOT to trade it.  
Market context, structure, timing, momentum, and discretion can make a huge difference, and those are difficult to fully capture with rigid mechanical rules.  
I’ve also spent months developing trading indicators and experimenting with AI-assisted analysis and automation.  
My current thinking is that AI’s biggest opportunity isn’t necessarily replacing discretionary traders or generating thousands of strategies.  
It’s learning to recognize the market conditions where a proven setup has the highest probability of working.  
Instead of asking AI, “What’s the next trade?”  
Maybe the better question is, “Is this actually the right environment for my strategy?”  
That’s the problem I find most interesting.

comments.author: StlnJones5107
comments.body:
I figured I'd share real numbers instead of screenshots. Nothing to sell, no course, no Discord.



\*\*Background\*\*



I'm a discretionary MES (Micro S&P futures) trader. I am not a programmer. Since September I've been building a bot, with Claude doing most of the architecture and code and ChatGPT used for second opinions and pushback. It runs on a small server, takes signals off 1-minute data and sends orders to Tradovate. It is still on a \*\*demo account\*\*. Live money is not on until it passes a checklist.

\*\*What the AI is actually good at\*\*

\- Writing and fixing the plumbing: order routing, placing a broker stop within a second of every fill, alerts, logs, a daily health report.

\- Testing ideas fast on 7 years of 1-minute MES data with real costs ($1.90 round trip plus slippage).

\- Telling me no. That turned out to be the most valuable part.

What it can't do is invent an edge. Everything it tested came from my own playbook.

\*\*What the testing showed\*\*

1. \*\*My opening range breakout (ORB) is the only thing with an edge so far, and it's thin.\*\* About +$2.33 per trade per MES after costs over \~1,300 trades, positive in the training period, the validation period and a holdout period nobody looked at until the end. That's roughly a few hundred dollars a year per contract with drawdowns over $1,000. Not a money printer. Real, though.

2. \*\*Most of my discretionary setups lost money as strict rules.\*\* Asia/London sweep and reclaim: negative. A VWAP fade from untested highs: 40 trades in 7 years, breakeven. When I checked my own tagged trades against the rules, the rules didn't match what I actually do. My edge in those trades is the judgment, and I haven't been able to write that down as numbers yet.

3. \*\*Some of my "rules" were wrong.\*\* I used to skip ORB when the market opened inside yesterday's value. Seven years of data said that filter wasn't reliable in either direction, so I dropped it.

4. \*\*The VIX filter I assumed was protecting me wasn't.\*\* Blocking trades at VIX 25+ didn't improve ORB (it actually did slightly better on high-VIX days), and on my overnight strategy it blocked the best recent trades.

5. \*\*A "flip test" is humbling.\*\* Run the exact same entries in the opposite direction. If the flipped version does about as well, you have a coin flip with good stops, not a directional edge.

\*\*How I test now\*\*

\- Write the rule and the pass/fail criteria down and commit them before running anything.

\- Three periods: build on one, check on a second, touch the third once at the end.

\- Costs and slippage in every test. Most ideas die right there.

\- One contract, demo account, every candidate and refusal logged, and a written error log for every bug and fix.

\*\*If you're starting with $100–$300\*\*

You can't trade futures with that and survive a normal losing streak. Paper trade one simple rule with fees for a few months first. Use AI to build and test, not to predict. If someone shows you +80% in a month, ask for the losing months.

replies.author: StlnJones5107
replies.body:
I don’t use a platform. Claude wrote the backtests in Python and I run them on a small research server, separate from the one that trades. Data is 7 years of 1-minute MES bars (May 2019 to Sept 2026) bought from Databento.

Every test simulates the trade bar by bar: entry on the next bar after the signal, a 10-point stop and the target checked every minute, and if the stop and target are hit in the same minute it counts as a stop. Costs are $1.90 round trip plus a quarter point of slippage on entries, stops and exits.

Before running anything I write the rules and the pass/fail rule down and commit them to GitHub, so I can’t tweak it after seeing the result. The data is split into three periods: 2019–2023 to build, 2023–2025 to check, and 2025–2026 touched once at the end. An idea has to make money in all three or it’s out. Most don’t make it.

Then it runs on a demo account, and I compare the live fills to what the backtest says should have happened.

comments.author: TradeyAI-R
comments.body:
We built TradeyAI for exactly this. You describe a strategy in plain language or copy a built-in one, and it turns that into rules that trade crypto and onchain US stocks. For live trading, you connect your own Binance account.

The issue we ran into early on: we let the LLM trade on its own, analyzing the market, social sentiment, and so on. But it made different decisions in the same situation, with different reasoning each time. That made the agent impossible to control or trust. 

So we changed the approach. Now the LLM helps turn your idea into clear rules, and those rules decide every trade. Each decision shows a checklist of which conditions were met and by how much, so when a strategy loses money, you can see exactly why. You can also backtest, chat with the agent to tweak settings, and paper trade before going live.

That said, I agree with what someone said above: AI can help you build and test a strategy, but it won't come up with a winning one for you. The edge still has to come from your own ideas.

comments.author: Ozymand7as
comments.body:
For the $100–$300 case, I’d make the first project an evaluation tool rather than a fully autonomous “AI trader.” Pick one simple rule set that you can explain clearly, then record every signal, the order you tried to send, the actual fill or rejection, fees, funding, and account balance over time.

The useful comparison is between the price when the signal fired and the price you could actually get. That is where a lot of backtests look much better than live trading, especially on low-liquidity coins or when the strategy trades often.

ChatGPT/Codex can help build the plumbing, tests, and logs. I would keep the strategy rules fixed during the paper-trading phase, though. If the rules, prompts, and parameters all keep changing, it becomes hard to tell whether there is any repeatable result at all.
